ORIGINAL CONTRIBUTION
The Occurrence of Stiff
Person Syndrome ina
Patient with Thymoma: Case
Report and Literature Review
By Semaan G. Kosseifi, MD; Jay B. Mehta, MD; Thomas Roy, MD; Ryland Byrd, Jr., MD; and Jeff Farrow, MD
ABSTRACT
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare dis-
order that affects the central nervous sys-
tem, being characterized by intermittent
episodes of muscle spasms, rigidity, and
a significant increase in morbidity and
mortality, We report a 29-year-old patient,
with left-sided chylothorax and thymoma,
who presented with truncal, lower ex-
tremities stiffness and painful cramps al-
leviated by diazepam and opiates. His
clinical picture was suggestive of SPS sec-
ondary to invasive thymoma. This syn-
drome is best approached by its early
recognition and prompt treatment since a
missed diagnosis can have deleterious
outcome. An intensive search for the un-
derlying etiology is of utmost importance
in the management of SPS. A review of the
current literature is also included in this
manuscript.
INTRODUCTION
The wide varieties of thymic diseases offer
a unique window to observe the complex
interaction leading to an autoimmune
diathesis. Stiff Person syndrome (SPS), is
a rare disorder that was first described by
Moersch and Woltman in 1956.' The syn-
drome is characterized by progressive
muscular stiffness and painful cramps that
can involve both axial and truncal mus-
cles, resulting in a significant morbidity
and mortality. Over 100 cases have been
published in the literature.’ An immuno-
logical basis of the syndrome can be en-
visaged, based on its association with
autoimmune diseases.’ Women appear to
be affected more often than men and this
might be reflected by the greater inci-
dence of immune-mediated disease re-
ported to occur more in women.
Symptoms usually begin between the third
and seventh decades of life; the onset of
the disease in childhood is rare.’ The de-
finitive mechanism for SPS is unclear but
it is hypothesized that it is mediated by im-
mune activation and production of IgG
antibody targeting both GABA-ergic neu-
rons and their nerve terminals as well as
beta cells of the pancreas. The most com-
mon autoantigen recognized by these au-
toantibodies was the glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) being present in
about 40-60 percent of patients with SPS.*
This case report emphasizes the need for
early diagnosis and prompt treatment
which may reduce morbidity and mortal-
ity associated with this syndrome. The fol-
lowing sections provide an overview of the
presentations, pathogenesis, diagnosis
and management of SPS.
CASE PRESENTATION
A 29-year-old previously healthy African-
American male patient complained of
four-week history of progressive shortness
of breath, non-productive cough and left-
sided chest pain. Chest radiograph re-
vealed complete opacification of the left
hemithorax with shift of the mediastinum
to the right (Figure 1). Computed tomog-
raphy of the chest demonstrated a large
left-sided pleural effusion and a large an-
terior mediastinal mass (Figure 2). The
patient underwent a left thoracocentesis.
Fluid analysis was suggestive of chylotho-
rax (milky appearance, triglycerides 1845
mg/dl with normal serum triglycerides,

FIGURE 2. Chest CT scan revealing a large

Cholesterol 27 mg/dl). PET scan
showed anterior mediastinal mass
with no significant increased activ-
ity. Laboratory data including blood,
urine, AFB’s were normal. Patient
underwent an open biopsy of the an-
terior mediastinal mass with the re-
sultant pathology specimen being
consistent with lymphocytic pre-
dominant epithelial type thymoma.
Due to the invasive behavior of this
neoplasm, an initial surgical treat-
ment was deferred and patient was
discharged home to be started on
four-drug-regimen chemotherapy
(Adriamycin, Cisplatin, Vincristine,
Cyclophosphamide) every three
weeks on an outpatient basis. Sev-
enty-two hours after discharge and
before receiving any chemotherapy,
the patient started having severe bi-
lateral lower extremity pain, muscle
cramps and weakness in both legs.
The patient did not have any short-
ness of breath, change in his bowel
habits, headache, double vision, dys-
phagia or other neurologic symp-
toms. Repeated physical
examination revealed evidence of an
unsteady antalgic gait, diffuse mus-
cular stiffness in both lower extrem-
ities along with diffuse lower back
pain. The rest of the neurologic ex-
amination was normal. Patient was
given diazepam 5 mg intravenously
along with intravenous morphine
with complete resolution of his
symptoms. In order to rule out other
associated disorders a full labora-
tory workup was done including a
paraneoplastic panel which included
anti-GAD antibodies; the result was
negative. Myasthenia gravis was
ruled out by a normal pulmonary
function test and a negative anti-
AChR antibodies test. Based on the
clinical picture, excluding other eti-
ologies, and the dramatic response
to benzodiazepine and opiates, the
diagnosis of SPS was made. Patient
received chemotherapy as planned
and at five-month follow up he did-
n’t have any recurrence of his symp-
toms with complete radiographic

DISCUSSION
SPS, since its early description, has been
found to be associated with a wide spec-
trum of clinical presentations, making its
diagnosis quite challenging. The associa-
tion of thymoma and SPS has been rarely
reported in the literature and, to our
knowledge, the total number of such
cases in the literature is nine, as summa-
rized in Table 1. The reason for these in-
teractions is unclear. The classic clinical
features of SPS consist of muscular stiff-
ness and rigidity as the name delineates.
Both axial and limb muscles can be in-
volved and can lead to spinal deformities
such as lordosis, which is thought to be
secondary to the simultaneous contrac-
tion of opposing paraspinal muscular
group, and stiff gait likened to that of
“Frankenstein's monster” as described in
1988.* Due the extreme degree of stiffness
patients may become bedridden and at
higher risks of recurrent falls and subse-
quent fractures. Muscle spasm and pain
are also characteristic features of SPS and
are usually episodic, easily visualized and
can be precipitated by both emotional and
mechanical stimuli producing rock-hard
appearance.' Moreover, investigators
found that the presence of head retraction
reflex can be an additional sign suggesting
the presence of this finding in a patient
with unexplained stiffness and spasms
might help avoid the otherwise frequent
misdiagnosis of a psychogenic motor dis-
turbance.’ Other reports have indicated
the association of seizure disorder and
depression in patients with SPS° which
were not present in our patient. Neuro-
logical findings such as autonomic dys-
function have been described in the
literature and if not recognized early may
result in poor outcome with increased
morbidities and even death.’ Rigidity and
spasm can involve respiratory muscles re-
sulting in tachypnea and respiratory fail-
ure.’ Swallowing and esophageal
dysfunction may lead to aspiration pneu-
monia.’ Other findings include specific
phobia and anxiety; both can exacerbate
rigidity and can also trigger spasms.'°

Despite advances in diagnostic modalities,
we still lack highly sensitive and specific
laboratory tests that can confirm the di-
agnosis of SPS. As a matter of fact, estab-
lishing the diagnosis of SPS requires a

high clinical suspicion. In a report pub-
lished in 1989, the authors, after review-
ing 13 patients over a 30-year period,
were able to define some diagnostic cri-
teria,!! summarized in Table 2. As is evi-
dent, and despite a negative anti- (GAD)
and anti-amphiphysin antibodies test, five
out of eight criteria were found in our pa-
tient, highly suggesting the diagnosis of
SPS. A list of the major differential diag-
noses that need to be considered in pa-
tients presenting with muscular
overactivity is provided in Table 3. These
include diseases such as Neuromyotonia,
also known as Isaac’s syndrome, which is
characterized by continuous muscle ac-
tivity on EMG, muscle stiffness similar to
SPS. The pathophysiology of Isaac’s syn-
drome is thought to be related to anti-
bodies directed against voltage-gated
potassium channels (VGKC) that can be
sporadic, or as a paraneoplastic disorder
related to malignancy, with thymoma
being one of the most commonly associ-
ated neoplasm, among others. Although
plasma exchange or intravenous im-
munoglobulin has been found to be ef-
fective for the treatment of Isaac’s
syndrome, other potentially effective treat-
ments include carbamazepine, diazepam
and phenytoin.
Chronic tetany as can be seen in
hypocalcemia, parathyroid disorders and
other disorders (hypomagnesemia, hy-
perphosphatemia, etc.) can also mimic
SPS and the diagnosis is usually made by
a prompt history and physical examina-
tion and laboratory findings. Startle dis-
ease, also known as hyperkeplexia or
congenital SPS, is an autosomal dominant
disorder characterized by an exaggerated
startle reaction to unexpected stimuli that
can lead to stiffness and sometimes fatal
hypertonia, especially in neonates. In
those cases, usually a family history along
with genetic studies and EMG findings can
help to differentiate from SPS. In addition,
Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigid-
ity and Myoclonus (PERM) may also sim-
ulate SPS, with the hallmark characteristic
of PREM being transient oculomotor dis-
turbances. Overlapping features have
been also reported, since some patients
with PREM were found to have positive
anti-GAD antibody, adding a challenging
flavor for confirming the diagnosis.
Moreover, myasthenic syndromes
have been reported to occur in patients
with thymoma.” For this reason it is cru-
cial to rule out such occurrences in pa-
tients presenting with weakness and
muscular dysfunction. In most cases, ap-

propriate history and examination along
with laboratory tests such as anti-AchR an-
tibody or antibodies against muscle-spe-
cific receptor tyrosine kinase (anti-MUSK
antibodies) can help in confirming the di-
agnosis. Other disorders such as neu-
roleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin
syndrome, metabolic myopathy, en-
docrine disorders (e.g., hyperthyroidism,
hypothyroidism, etc.), rhabdomyolysis
and other neuromuscular diseases also
need to be excluded, and in those entities
a complete clinical and laboratory
workup will help to differentiate them.
The treatment of SPS is a combination
of both symptomatic and etiology-based
therapy. Benzodiazepine, by modulating
the activity and levels of GABA, was shown
to be very effective for symptom relief and
the most widely used drug is diazepam."
In most cases, benzodiazepine treatment
is started first with escalating doses to
reach clinical improvement. In benzodi-
azepine-resistant cases or in cases of doc-
umented toxicity it is recommended to
switch to baclofen, which is also a GABA
modulating drug, as monotherapy or add
baclofen to the benzodiazepine. Baclofen
can be administered orally (20 mg BID or
TID) or via an intrathecal route. Compli-
cations of the procedure included spasm-
induced rupture and dislocation of the
intrathecal catheter.'*
A number of other potential therapies
have been tried anecdotally in SPS. These
include the muscle relaxant methocar-
bamol given intravenously, botulinum
toxin A (injected into the paraspinal mus-
cles), sodium valproate, and vigabatrin.
The role of these agents is unclear.
In selected cases where glucocorti-
coids cannot be used or are associated
with severe complications (glaucoma, se-
vere osteoporosis, hyperglycemia given
the association of type 1 diabetes with
SPS/SMS2 or severe psychosis), or in glu-
cocorticoids-resistant cases, alternative
drug therapies might be required. Im-
munosuppressive therapy should be con-
sidered in those patients. Azathioprine has
been used as a steroid-sparing agent in
some cases. In other refractory cases in-
travenous immnuglobulin have been used
with promising results in severe cases.
Other treatment options in patients with
life threatening symptoms such as plasma-
pheresis and the chimeric pan-B cell
(anti-CD20) monoclonal antibody, ritux-
imab, have also been used and provided
provide benefit in the occasional patients
pending further studies.
Equally important is the etiology-
based therapy and, as reviewed in Table
1, most of the reviewed patients under-
went thymomectomy. In our patient, sur-
gical therapy was not an option because

of the aggressive behavior of the thymoma

invading surrounding structures, and the
decision was to opt for a chemotherapy
trial with good clinical and radiographic

The prognosis for patients with SPS is
still variable and unpredictable, with the
functional status being dependent on
whether patients will have a limited or
more extensive multi-systemic involve-
ment. Patients with more limited disease
may continue to function normally for ex-
tended periods of time.’ Importantly, cli-
nicians from all specialties may encounter
SPS and need to familiarize themselves
with the salient features about the syn-
drome and its management. As we men-
tion earlier in the manuscript, the
awareness of the clinician to the associa-
tion of SPS with type 1 diabetes mellitus
and/or malignancy is of utmost impor-
tance and requires a specific attention for
these diagnoses.
CURRENT STATE OF KNOWLEDGE AND
FUTURE RESEARCH NEEDS
Thymoma and SPS can coexist leading to
enormous morbidity. Pathophysiologi-
cally, the two conditions seem to overlap
significantly, as autoimmune and parane-
oplastic processes are pivotal aspects of
both disorders. It is important for the cli-
nician taking care of these complicated
patients to be aware of this association
and to carry out appropriate diagnostic
and treatment strategies. The association
of thymoma and SPS, though described
anecdotally, has not been systematically
studied, partly because the rarity of such
association means it is easily overlooked.
Based on the above discussion, a detailed
analysis of the thymoma/SPS association
is needed to further understand the cor-
relation between the two diseases as well
as other existing co-morbidities, and to
possibly set forth further management
goals and future areas of research. Since
genetic factors are involved in the patho-
genesis of SPS, relatives should be in-
structed about SPS and their enhanced
risk of developing the syndrome." A high
index of suspicion is needed for early di-
agnosis of SPS since it could have delete-
rious and potentially fatal effects due to

major organ dysfunction if not early diag-
nosed and appropriately treated. In our
patient the early recognition and treat-
ment management led to rapid recovery.
In particular, the following pivotal is-
sues may need to be addressed in re-
search studies:
. Moersch FP, Woltman HW:
1. Newer serological markers that im-
prove the diagnostic yields need to
be studied further.
2. Better understanding of the patho-
physiology and the need for sero-
logic markers that can predict
complications still need to be eval-
uated.
